questions.question: In CBC mode, what does a plaintext block depend on during decryption?
options: The block decryption of the current ciphertext XORed with the previous ciphertext (or IV)
Only the current ciphertext block (CBC is not chained during decryption)
Only the IV (the ciphertext is used only for integrity)
The sum of all previous plaintext blocks (CBC is additive)
questions.explanation: CBC decryption is P_i = D_K(C_i) XOR C_{i-1}, with C_0 = IV.

questions.question: What is a padding oracle, in the attacker’s view?
options: Any observable signal that correlates with whether decrypted padding is valid
A server endpoint that returns the decrypted plaintext
A public key that allows anyone to decrypt CBC ciphertexts
A random-number generator used to create padding bytes
questions.explanation: The attacker only needs a yes/no (or distinguishable) signal tied to padding validity.

questions.question: Why does changing the IV (or C_{i-1}) let an attacker control bytes of P_i in CBC decryption?
options: Because P_i is XORed with the IV/previous ciphertext after block decryption
Because the block cipher key is derived from the IV
Because the IV is encrypted with ECB before use
Because CBC decryption reuses the same block twice
questions.explanation: In CBC, the XOR with IV/C_{i-1} happens after D_K(C_i), so flipping bits flips plaintext bits.

questions.question: In a byte-at-a-time padding oracle attack, what does a “valid padding” response tell you?
options: Your trial IV/C_{i-1} produced a plaintext suffix matching the required padding pattern
You found the encryption key
The ciphertext was not modified in transit
The plaintext is ASCII and therefore parseable
questions.explanation: Valid padding means the decrypted block ends in 0x01 or 0x02 0x02, etc., which leaks information.

questions.question: When targeting pad_len = 3, how do you set already-recovered trailing bytes in the trial IV/C_{i-1}?
options: Force each trailing plaintext byte to equal 0x03 by XORing with (known intermediate) and 0x03
Leave them unchanged; only the new byte matters
Set them all to 0x00 so the block becomes zeroed
Randomize them each query to avoid detection
questions.explanation: You must adjust previously solved positions so the block ends with 0x03 0x03 0x03.

questions.question: Which defense actually prevents the padding oracle in legacy CBC designs?
options: Authenticate ciphertexts and verify the MAC before decrypting/unpadding, with indistinguishable errors
Add random sleep on padding failure
Base64-encode ciphertexts before decrypting
Use a longer IV
questions.explanation: Verify integrity first (encrypt-then-authenticate) and avoid distinguishable failure signals.

questions.question: What is the best modern replacement for CBC+PKCS#7 in new systems?
options: An AEAD mode like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305
ECB with a random IV
CBC with a secret IV
A custom padding scheme with randomized bytes
questions.explanation: AEAD provides confidentiality and integrity in one construction and avoids padding-oracle footguns.

questions.question: Why is “add random delay on failure” an unreliable padding-oracle mitigation?
options: The signal often remains statistically distinguishable with enough samples
It makes the ciphertext immutable
It prevents chosen-ciphertext queries entirely
It changes CBC into an AEAD mode
questions.explanation: Noise can reduce signal strength, but attackers can average it out; the oracle often still exists.
